title: Chaos in the double pendulum at every energy
W: The planar double pendulum with equal masses and equal arms looks chaotic at moderate energies but almost regular at very low and very high energies. Prove that it has genuine (positive-entropy) chaos at every energy above the rest state.
M: Let $H(\theta_1,\theta_2,p_1,p_2)$ be the Hamiltonian of the planar double pendulum with $m_1=m_2=\ell_1=\ell_2=g=1$ on $T^*\mathbb T^2$, with minimum value $E_0$ (the hanging rest state). Prove that for every $E>E_0$ the Hamiltonian flow restricted to $\{H=E\}$ has positive topological entropy.
why: The double pendulum is the standard textbook example of chaos, yet rigorous chaos is not known uniformly in energy. Both ends are near-integrable: at low energy it is a nonresonant pair of oscillators (frequency ratio 1+sqrt2), and at high energy it is nearly free rotation. Chaos there needs exponentially small splitting estimates, and the middle range needs computer-assisted proofs, so it is a concrete test for both techniques.
notes: Question is qualitative (positive topological entropy at every energy); no natural numeric quantity whose bounds carry the content. Energy-threshold variants would be arbitrary.

title: Closed-form Euler blow-up
W: Smooth compactly supported starting data for the 3D Euler equations that blow up in finite time are now known to exist, but the construction is an infinite iterative series. Give such data as an explicit formula.
M: Find an explicit divergence-free $u_0=\nabla\times\big(P(x)e^{-|x|^2}\big)$ with $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]^3$ (or another explicitly specified finite closed-form class) such that the unforced 3D incompressible Euler solution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has finite maximal smooth lifespan.
why: An explicit blow-up datum would let the singularity be checked numerically and studied concretely, beyond pure existence. It is a refinement of the now-resolved existence question.
notes: No natural bound quantity; closed-form class is arbitrary. No honest C-to-B fix found: core existence question is resolved and residual explicitness variants remain arbitrary.

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
W: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
M: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.
why: This asks for a volume 'law of large numbers' along a deterministic, uniquely ergodic substitution sequence, the analogue of Viaggi's theorem for random mapping tori.
notes: Limit value is not a natural constant. C-to-B attempt (general uniquely ergodic substitutions) still looks routine via almost-additivity of mapping-torus volume plus subadditive ergodic arguments; leave C.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
W: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
M: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)
why: Joining the c trees with c - 1 new edges makes a single tree, and a graceful labelling of that tree restricts to such a labelling of the forest. So this statement follows from the Graceful Tree Conjecture (Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa) but is weaker than it. The best unconditional results only give labels in {1,...,(1+eps)n}, or (1-eps)n distinct differences, so even one spare label for every tree would be new progress.
notes: Bound formulation is already standard: gracesize of trees, gs(T)>=(1-eps)n (Letzter-Pokrovskiy-Williams, arXiv 2511.11331), range-relaxed labellings (Van Bussel 2002). Famous-problem bound, excluded by rule.

title: Fibonacci-modulated growing Jacobi matrix
W: Take a Jacobi matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal weights sqrt(n). Double the weight at every position where the Fibonacci word has a 1. Periodic modulations of power-growing weights are known to produce spectral phase transitions. Determine the spectral type for this aperiodic modulation.
M: Let $f=f_1f_2f_3\cdots=0100101001001\cdots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ be the Fibonacci word, the fixed point of $0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0$. Let $J$ be the Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $(Ju)_n=a_{n-1}u_{n-1}+a_nu_{n+1}$, where $a_n=\sqrt n\,(1+f_n)$ and $a_0u_0:=0$. Since $\sum 1/a_n=\infty$, $J$ is self-adjoint (Carleman). Determine the spectral type of $J$. In particular: is $\sigma_{ac}(J)\neq\emptyset$? Is $\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$? Is the spectrum on some interval pure point or singular continuous?
why: Janas, Naboko, Swiderski and others classified unbounded Jacobi matrices with periodically modulated power-growing weights. Whether the spectrum is absolutely continuous, a gap, or point spectrum is decided by the trace of a single period's transfer matrix. A Fibonacci modulation joins this theory to the trace-map dynamics of quasicrystal Schrodinger operators. In that setting the period matrix is replaced by a hierarchy of block products.
notes: Question asks for spectral type; exponent 1/2 and factor 2 are arbitrary, and no natural quantity with known bounds exists.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
W: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
M: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)
why: Khalfalah and Szemeredi proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic pair x != y with x+y a square; this asks for the next configuration, a monochromatic triangle in the 'square-sum graph'. Density arguments fail (residue classes such as n = 1 mod 3 contain no such triangle), so a proof must be genuinely Ramsey-theoretic, in the same family as the open Pythagorean-triple and {x,y,x+y,xy} problems.
notes: Only numeric candidate is the r=2 threshold in (8000,10000], which is an arbitrary computational instance and not a natural constant. Content is qualitative (infinite chromatic number).

title: Minimal degree of a three-variable Jacobian counterexample
quantity: d_3 = least max-component degree of a non-injective Keller map C^3 -> C^3
lower: d_3 >= 3: Wang (1980), every Keller map of degree <= 2 is invertible in any dimension (restated in arXiv 2608.00222).
upper: d_3 <= 7: Alpoge's map, component degrees (7,6,4), det JF = -2 (arXiv 2608.00222 Thm 3.3; elementary rederivation arXiv 2609.17795; Isabelle AFP Jacobian_Counterexample).
W: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpoge's map has component degrees 7, 6, 4), and Wang's theorem rules out degree 2. Determine the smallest possible degree, or at least narrow the range 3 to 7: either find a counterexample of degree at most 6, or prove that every counterexample has degree at least 4 (every cubic Keller map of C^3 is invertible).
M: Call $F\in\mathbb C[x,y,z]^3$ a Keller map if $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, and set $\deg F=\max_i\deg F_i$. Let $d_3=\min\{\deg F: F\text{ Keller, not injective on }\mathbb C^3\}$. Known: $3\le d_3\le 7$. Improve either bound: exhibit a non-injective Keller map with $\deg F\le 6$, or prove $d_3\ge 4$ (equivalently, every Keller map $\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ of degree $\le3$ is invertible), or determine $d_3$.
why: Now that JC_3 fails, the size of the smallest failure separates the low-degree range where invertibility can still be proved (Wang's degree 2; cubic-homogeneous x+H in dimension 3) from the range where counterexamples live. Bass-Connell-Wright reductions raise the dimension, so degree in dimension 3 is a separate question. Both directions are checkable: an explicit map is verified by computer algebra, and a lower bound is a theorem.
notes: Searched 2026 papers (2608.00222, 2609.17795, 2607.18186, 2607.22198, 2610.35918): none gives a degree <7 example in C^3 or settles the cubic case. 2607.18186 says its 79-variable cubic bound is not an optimization. Risk: computer search might settle quickly.

title: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
upper: delta_tau <= 2: Fredman (1976), any set G of permutations can be sorted with log2|G| + 2n comparisons. Opler (arXiv 2409.07868) gives O((log c_tau +1)n), optimal only up to a constant factor. delta_tau = 0 is known for tau of length 3 in the 132-class (stack sorting, <=2n vs log2 C_n = 2n - O(log n)).
W: Sorting an array promised to avoid a fixed pattern needs at least log2 of the number of allowed orders comparisons, and Fredman's theorem says 2n more always suffice. How many extra comparisons per element are really needed? Show that fewer than 2n extra suffice for 1324-avoiding inputs, or show that a linear excess is necessary for some pattern.
M: For a permutation $\tau$ let $C_\tau(n)$ be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing $\tau$) that sorts $a_1,\dots,a_n$ under the promise that their order pattern lies in $\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)$. Let $\delta_\tau=\limsup_n (C_\tau(n)-\log_2|\mathrm{Av}_n(\tau)|)/n$. Known: $0\le\delta_\tau\le2$ (Fredman). Improve either bound for some $\tau$ of length 4, in particular prove $\delta_{1324}<2$, or find $\tau$ with $\delta_\tau>0$. Is $\delta_\tau=0$ for every $\tau$?
why: The comparison model is one of the few places where information-theoretic lower bounds are nearly exact, yet even for unrestricted sorting it is unknown whether log2 n! + o(n) suffices. Pattern classes give a structured family where the excess is quantifiable. Upper-side progress needs a structure-aware algorithm beating the generic Fredman bound, and lower-side progress would need a new adversary technique.
notes: Opler's abstract checked: it gives no additive-excess constant. Generic Fredman excess cannot be improved for arbitrary sets of permutations, so any delta<2 needs class structure. The upper side for specific length-4 patterns may be moderately accessible.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
quantity: m(P) Ramsey multiplicity of Petersen graph
W: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
M: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.
why: Which graphs are common (random coloring is optimal) is a central question in Ramsey multiplicity. The known obstructions (containing $K_4$, the Turán-coloring criterion of Fox–Wigderson) do not apply to the triangle-free, girth-5, 3-chromatic Petersen graph. It is a natural test case, between odd cycles (common) and graphs containing $K_4$ (uncommon).
notes: Upper bound 2^{-14} is random colouring; no reliable published nontrivial lower bound on m(P) found, and the content is the commonness yes/no. Cannot pin down lower bound.

title: Two-frequency localization
W: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
M: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).
why: Multi-frequency localization at large coupling is known only for a full-measure set of frequency vectors, because the proofs (Bourgain-Goldstein, Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag) delete frequencies by semi-algebraic elimination. Proving it for one explicit Diophantine vector such as (√2,√3), which is Diophantine by Schmidt's subspace theorem, would require an arithmetic way to control double resonances, as Jitomirskaya's method does for one frequency.
notes: Content is qualitative (localization at fixed frequency vector); lambda_0 is inexplicit in every method and is not a natural constant to bound.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
quantity: k(n) minimal edge types for uniquely assembling n x n jigsaw
lower: k(n) >= (sqrt(n)-1)/2 by counting: n^2 distinct pieces <= (2k+1)^4 label types
upper: self-proved k(n) <= 2n(n-1) (all edges distinct); O(n) plausible by adapting Martinsson (arXiv 1701.04813) but his model differs
W: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
M: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?
why: Uniqueness of jigsaw reconstruction is a well-studied model problem for shotgun assembly (Mossel–Ross; Bordenave–Feige–Mossel; Nenadov–Pfister–Steger), but all known thresholds concern random puzzles, where about n edge types are needed. Since unique assembly forces all n^2 pieces to be distinct, a simple count gives k(n) ≥ c√n, so the question is whether designed puzzles can beat random ones by a polynomial factor, a rigidity/design question in the spirit of de Bruijn tori.
notes: Martinsson model colours border edges and uses involution-paired jigs; transfer to flat borders and exact uniqueness not verified. Best upper bound cannot be pinned reliably, and a routine sqrt(n) construction is a risk.
